newsitem.title: USA: U.S. May CPI yet another snapshot of low inflation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. May CPI yet another snapshot of low inflation.

text.p: A slight increase in the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) in May was in line with forecasts and offered one more snapshot of a low-inflation U.S. economy, economists said.
The Labor Department reported that the CPI rose 0.1 percent in May overall. Without its more volatile food and energy components, the core CPI rose 0.2 percent.
"The CPI is just more good news," said Sally Kleinman, economist at Chase Securities Inc. "There was really nothing in the report ... at all surprising. There's no inflation."
Economists polled by Reuters had anticipated, on average, a 0.2 percent increase in both the overall and core rates.
In April, the CPI rose 0.1 percent and the core index increased 0.3 percent.

The bond market reacted little to the report at first, then weakened on profit-taking. Analysts said the market had already priced in the friendly inflation numbers, which are the latest in a long stream of such reports.
"(The CPI was) a very favorable report," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co: "A lot of it was built into the marketplace."

"It was an excellent number," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "It was on expectations, which probably accounts for the fact that the market's not doing anything with the numbers."
At 0910 EDT/1310 GMT, 40 minutes after the CPI was released, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 6/32 to 98-29/32, yielding 6.71 percent.
"The market geared up for the CPI yesterday," said Platt, referring to the bond market's advance on Monday.
"The market needs surprisingly friendly information in order to keep lurching forward," he said.
Strauss of Sanwa said many of the individual components of the report behaved well.

"We got a tempering in the apparel price hike, which was expected. We got some pickup in food prices, which was (also) expected, (but) that was more than offset by a big drop in energy prices," he said.
Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc, said the report showed that inflation was low in May.
"So far in June, we don't have any indications that anything has changed with regard to that (low inflation picture)," he said.

"Neither commodity prices nor anecdotal reports from companies on their ability to raise prices indicate that inflation is picking up at all in June," said Worseck. "But we still think wage increases will put very modest upward pressure on the CPI later this year and that that will force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point later this year.

"We think the economy will do better in the second half of the year," Worseck said. "Consumer confidence is very high. People are still getting jobs and you still could get a pickup in the economy in the third quarter."
